lesson.title: Loaded Words, Different Answers: The Power of Question Wording
lesson.summary: The exact phrasing of a survey question can swing results by dozens of percentage points, making wording one of the most controllable and most abused sources of response bias.
lesson.body:
Wording of questions is the most controllable, and most frequently abused, source of response bias. Two surveys can draw identical simple random samples from the same population and still produce wildly different results, purely because one used charged language and the other used neutral language. Where the previous chapter asked why respondents might not tell the truth, this chapter asks a narrower and more practical question: how does the exact phrasing on the page change what respondents say, even when they are trying to answer honestly?

Several specific wording problems recur constantly. Leading or loaded questions embed an opinion inside the question itself, such as asking whether people support wasteful government spending rather than simply asking about spending levels. Double barreled questions ask about two things at once, such as whether a respondent supports lower taxes and smaller government, forcing a single answer onto two possibly different opinions. Unfamiliar or technical vocabulary confuses respondents into guessing. Question order matters as well, because an earlier question can anchor how someone interprets a later one. Even the order and balance of answer choices can nudge responses, since people often pick options presented first or ones that sound more socially acceptable.

Imagine a school district wants to gauge support for a budget proposal and tests two versions of the same underlying question on comparable groups of parents. Version A asks whether parents support cutting government waste in the school budget. Version B asks whether parents support cutting the school budget for education programs and after school activities. These describe roughly the same policy, but the emotional weight of the words waste versus education programs points respondents toward very different answers.

Suppose Version A produces 74 percent yes, 18 percent no, and 8 percent undecided, while Version B produces 31 percent yes, 55 percent no, and 14 percent undecided. Within each version the three categories are disjoint and must account for every respondent, so the addition rule confirms the tallies are complete. For Version A, P(yes or undecided) = P(yes) + P(undecided) = 0.74 + 0.08 = 0.82, so by the complement rule, P(no) = 1 minus 0.82 = 0.18, exactly matching the reported figure. For Version B, P(yes or undecided) = 0.31 + 0.14 = 0.45, so P(no) = 1 minus 0.45 = 0.55, again matching. The forty three percentage point swing in the yes response, from 74 percent down to 31 percent, comes entirely from wording, since nothing about the underlying sample or the actual policy changed.

Professional survey organizations guard against these effects with pilot testing, sometimes called cognitive interviewing, where a small group of respondents talks through how they interpreted each question before it goes out widely. Good practice also means neutral, familiar language, avoiding double barreled questions, balancing the answer choices so no option is favored by its position, and where possible randomizing question order across respondents so order effects average out rather than favoring one answer.

Wording is powerful precisely because it is invisible to most respondents, who assume the question in front of them is neutral even when it is not. The next chapter pulls this thread together with everything covered so far, since designing a trustworthy survey means controlling the sample, the coverage, the response rate, and the wording all at once, not fixing one problem while leaving the others unaddressed.
